newsitem.title: UK: MOTOR RACING-HILL AND WALKINSHAW COULD STUN THE SCEPTICS.
newsitem.headline: MOTOR RACING-HILL AND WALKINSHAW COULD STUN THE SCEPTICS.

text.p: Damon Hill surprised motor sport when he signed for Tom Walkinshaw's Arrows team but the two are proven winners and could form the perfect partnership.
Walkinshaw, who recently acquired the ailing Arrows grand prix team, had stalked his prey with all the care to be expected of a Scottish farmer's son.

"I spoke to him at Monza, once the divorce from Williams was announced," he said. "But I told him not to contact me until he was serious. I didn't want to be part of the speculation and all the musical chairs' business that goes on in Formula One."

When Hill did phone, a meeting was arranged. He visited Walkinshaw's headquarters, a 15 million pounds ($23.48 million) investment set in rolling English countryside west of Oxford, and asked a stream of questions.
Hill was impressed by the state-of-the-art set-up. He promptly signed a one-year deal for the 1997 world championship and the hunt was over.

Last week's announcement came as a shock and even Damon's wife Georgie was surprised by both the alacrity and the identity of the Scot who was to become her husband's boss. Elsewhere, there was widespread incredulity that the man who could become world champion a week on Sunday had opted for such an unsuccessful team.
Ambitious, hard-working, meticulous in his planning and his engineering and immersed in the business, industry and sport of motor racing, Walkinshaw has been called many things in his time.

But few of even the most barbed descriptions have penetrated his hide. As a successful driver, he raced in Formula Ford, Formula Three, Formula Two and then won two European saloon car championships with Jaguar.

While driving for Jaguar he learned about management and finally took control of their hugely successful sportscar team. Winning came naturally -- Le Mans, Silverstone, Daytona...seemingly everywhere.
He switched to Formula One and in 1994 helped to guide Michael Schumacher and Benetton to the world drivers' title
After that, Walkinshaw moved on to Ligier before French frustrations led him to buy the cash-strapped Footwork Arrows operation this year.

He may be ruthless and demanding, but his track record is golden and shimmers in sponsors' eyes. Those who work for him talk without reservation of his charisma, commonsense and loyalty. Above all, Walkinshaw is a leader, and a man who delivers what he promises.
"He always sticks to the facts," said Richard Grundy, Formula One marketing manager at TWR Arrows.
"He does not chase dreams. He is only interested in what is realistic and feasible. But he also has tremendous courage and will follow things through, right to the end.

"In short, he is a great man to work for as I am sure Damon has realised. I think he is an inspiring individual to work for. He commands respect, he is very supportive, he gives everyone very clear goals and objectives and then he leaves you alone to get on with it."

Walkinshaw, 50, father-of-two, lives in rural comfort on a sprawling farm. He has amassed an estimated 40 million pounds ($62.62 million) fortune from his 20-year-old TWR Group, an international company with a 250 million pounds ($391.million) turnover and staff of more than 1,200.
The group is a world leader in automotive design, engineering and manufacturing with a client list that includes Volvo, Aston Martin, General Motors, Mitsubishi, Jaguar and Ford.
His activities are wide-reaching and energetic and his Formula One involvement with Arrows is the culmination of several years' search to find the right opportunity.
It is a measure of Walkinshaw's ability, marketing skills and ambitions that Hill chose him ahead of Jackie Stewart and his brand new team and Jordan, now in its sixth year at the top.
